title: Ten Weeks to the Marathon

lines.text: Right, Diego, the race is ten weeks away, so let's look at your training plan. Are you ready?
I think so. I'm a bit nervous, to be honest. I've never run more than twenty kilometres.
That's normal. By the end of next month, you'll have run thirty kilometres at least once. I promise.
Thirty? Wow. So what will I be doing in the first few weeks?
For the first three weeks, you'll be running four times a week. Three short runs and one long run on Sundays.
And what about the gym? Will I be lifting weights as well?
Yes, twice a week, but nothing too heavy. We want strong legs, not tired legs.
Okay. And when will I be doing the really long runs?
In weeks five to eight. By week eight, you'll have completed three runs of over thirty kilometres. After that, we'll slow down.
Slow down? Just before the race?
Exactly. In the last two weeks, you'll be resting more and eating lots of pasta and rice. Your body needs to recover.
That sounds like the best part of the plan! What time does the race start, by the way?
At six in the morning. So this time in ten weeks, you'll be standing at the start line, probably feeling very excited.
And by lunchtime I'll have finished, I hope!
If you follow the plan, you'll have finished long before lunch. Most runners at your level take about four hours.
Four hours. Okay. I'll be thinking about that pasta the whole way.

title: Walking the Golden Gate

lines.text: Good morning, everyone, and welcome to the Golden Gate Bridge. Please stay together on the walkway and watch out for bikes.
The bridge was opened in nineteen thirty-seven. At that time, it was the longest bridge of its kind in the world.
How long did it take to build?
The work was started in nineteen thirty-three, so it was finished in about four years. Thousands of workers were employed, and a safety net was hung under the bridge to protect them.
And what about the colour? Was it always orange?
Good question. The steel was covered in a red-orange paint to protect it, and people liked it so much that it was never changed. The colour is called International Orange.
Interestingly, the Navy wanted it to be painted black and yellow, so that it could be seen more easily by ships.
Is it being painted right now? I can see some people up there.
Yes, it's being painted all the time. A team of painters works on it every day, because the salty air damages the metal.
Since it opened, the bridge has been crossed by more than two billion vehicles.
That's amazing. Has it ever been closed because of the weather?
Only a few times. It has been closed because of very strong winds, but that doesn't happen often.
The fog, on the other hand, is very common, especially in summer. On some days the towers can't be seen at all.
I hope we can see them today!
We're lucky this morning. In a few minutes, a group photo will be taken at the next viewpoint, and after that you'll be given free time to walk to the other side.
Will the photos be sent to us by email?
Yes, they'll be sent tonight. Okay, let's keep walking.

dictation: Please stay together on the walkway and watch out for bikes.
The fog, on the other hand, is very common, especially in summer.

title: The Bus Broke Down
focus: Time clauses (as soon as, by the time, until)

lines.text: Hello?
Hello, Mr Vargas? This is Laura Pineda, Sofía's teacher. Don't worry, everyone's fine, but I'm calling about the school trip.
Oh, okay. Is something wrong?
The bus broke down about an hour ago, on the road back from Villa de Leyva. We're waiting at a petrol station until the mechanic arrives.
I see. When do you think you'll get back to Bogotá?
Well, the mechanic says he'll be here by four. As soon as he checks the engine, he'll tell us if he can fix it.
And if he can't?
Then the company will send another bus. But by the time it gets here, it'll probably be dark, so we might arrive quite late.
How late are we talking about?
Maybe around nine. I'll send a message to all the parents as soon as I know more.
Thanks. Are the kids okay? Do they have food?
Yes, they're fine. They're eating snacks and playing cards. We won't leave the petrol station until we're sure the bus is safe.
That's the most important thing. Should I wait at the school, then?
Yes, please, but don't leave home until you receive my message. There's no point waiting outside in the cold for hours.
Okay. And please tell Sofía to call me when she gets a chance.
Of course. I'll tell her as soon as I hang up. Thanks for understanding, Mr Vargas.

title: What Would You Do with a Free Year?

lines.text: Welcome back to Coffee Break Questions. I'm Hannah.
And I'm Josh. Today's question comes from a listener in Cali: if you had a whole year free, with enough money, what would you do?
Ooh, that's a good one. Honestly, if I had a free year, I'd travel across South America by bus.
By bus? Wouldn't that be really tiring?
Maybe, but if I flew everywhere, I wouldn't see the small towns. I'd start in Patagonia and finish in the north of Colombia.
That sounds amazing. If I were you, I'd learn some Spanish first, though.
Definitely. What about you, Josh? What would you do?
I think I'd learn to cook properly. If I had more time, I wouldn't eat toast for dinner three nights a week.
Toast for dinner? Josh, that's terrible!
I know! So I'd spend six months in Italy and six months in Mexico, taking cooking classes.
And would you open a restaurant when you came back?
No way. If I opened a restaurant, I'd never have a free year again!
Fair point. We also asked some listeners. Marta told us that if she didn't have to work, she'd volunteer at an animal shelter.
And Luis said he'd write a novel. He's had the idea for years, but he never has time.
So, what would you do if you had a free year? Send us a message and we'll read the best answers next week.
See you then!

title: The Final We Nearly Won

lines.text: Hey, Mateo. I heard about the final on Saturday. I'm really sorry.
Thanks. I still can't stop thinking about it. We lost two-one in the last minute.
What happened? You were winning at half-time, weren't you?
Yes, one-nil. If I had scored that penalty in the second half, we would have won easily.
You missed a penalty? Oh no.
I hit the post. If I'd kicked it a bit more to the left, it would have gone in.
Come on, it wasn't only your fault. What about the rest of the team?
Well, our goalkeeper was ill, so a defender played in goal. If Carlos had been there, he would have stopped that last goal for sure.
Exactly. So it was bad luck, not just you.
Maybe. And our coach was angry with the referee. He said that if the referee had seen the foul on Andrés, we would have got a free kick.
Honestly, if you hadn't played so well in the semi-final, you wouldn't have been in the final at all.
That's true. I hadn't thought about it like that.
And remember, last year you didn't even get past the first round.
Ha, you're right. We've improved a lot.
So stop worrying. Next year you'll win it. And you'll practise penalties every day, right?
Every single day. I promise.

title: The Neighbour Upstairs

lines.text: So, did you finally talk to the neighbour upstairs?
Yes, I did, this morning. I knocked on her door and told her that the music had kept me awake all week.
And what did she say?
She said she was really sorry. She told me that she hadn't realised the walls were so thin.
Well, that's a good start. Did she explain why she plays music so late?
Yes. She said she worked night shifts at a hospital and that music helped her relax when she got home.
Oh, I didn't know that. That makes it a bit more understandable.
Exactly. Then she asked me what time I usually went to bed.
What did you tell her?
I said I went to bed at about eleven because I had to get up at six. Then she asked if headphones would be okay.
Headphones? That's a perfect solution.
That's what I said. She also asked whether I wanted to come for coffee on Sunday.
Really? So now you're friends?
Maybe! She told me she had moved to the city only two months ago and didn't know anyone yet.
Well, I think you handled it really well. I would have just complained to the building manager.
I thought about it, but my mum always told me that a conversation was better than a complaint.

title: The Arepa Truck

lines.text: Today I'm talking to Jorge Castaño, the man who runs La Arepería Rodante, a food truck that has become famous in Miami. Jorge, welcome.
Thanks, Olivia. It's great to be here.
So, tell us about the truck. Where did it come from?
It's an old ice cream truck, which I bought from a retired couple in Florida. It was the only one that I could afford.
And who taught you to make arepas?
My grandmother, who lived in Medellín all her life. She had a little shop where she sold arepas every morning.
What makes your arepas different?
We use corn that we grind ourselves every day. And the cheese, which comes from a small farm in Georgia, is very similar to Colombian cheese.
Who are your customers? Are they mostly Colombians?
Not at all. We get students who want something cheap, office workers who are in a hurry, and tourists who have never tried an arepa.
Is there a dish that everyone orders?
Yes, the arepa de choclo, which is a sweet corn arepa with cheese. People who try it usually come back the next day.
And where can people find you?
We park near the university on weekdays. On Saturdays we go to Wynwood, where there's a big market.
Jorge, thank you. I know where I'm having lunch today!

title: When Grandpa Was My Age
focus: used to / would / be used to

lines.text: Grandpa, can I ask you some questions for my school project? It's about how Bogotá has changed.
Of course, sweetheart. Go ahead.
How did you use to get to school when you were my age?
I used to walk. It took forty minutes, because nobody had a car in our family. My brothers and I would race each other down the hill.
Forty minutes! Didn't you get tired?
Not really. We were used to it. Children walked everywhere back then.
What did you use to do in your free time?
On Sundays, we would go to the park with a ball and play until it got dark. There were no mobile phones, so our mother used to whistle when it was time for dinner.
Did Bogotá use to be as big as it is now?
Not at all. Lots of the neighbourhoods you know were farms. I remember cows near where the shopping centre is today.
Wow. Is there anything you miss?
I miss the quiet. I'm still not used to all the traffic and noise, even after all these years.
And is there anything that's better now?
Oh yes, the TransMilenio! I'm used to taking it now, and it's much faster than the old buses. And of course, I can video call your cousins in Spain.
Thanks, Grandpa. This is going to be the best project in the class.

title: Whose Phone Is This?

lines.text: Sam, look. Someone's left a phone on this table.

title: The Seven-Day Phone Challenge

lines.text: Hello, and welcome to the Seven-Day Phone Challenge. My name's Emma, and this week I'm going to help you spend less time on your screen.
First, let's be honest. Most of us can't stop checking our phones. Some people pick them up more than a hundred times a day.
On day one, I want you to turn off all your notifications, except calls and messages from your family. You'll be surprised how quiet your life becomes.
On day two, try leaving your phone in another room while you eat. Enjoy talking to the people around you instead.
On day three, decide to stop using your phone one hour before bed. Reading a book is a great way to relax.
Many people tell me they're afraid of missing important news. Don't worry. If it's really important, someone will call you.
On day four, avoid opening social media before lunch. If you need to know the time, use a watch.
Day five is my favourite. Plan to meet a friend face to face, and agree to put both phones away.
On day six, practise doing nothing for ten minutes. It sounds strange, but your brain needs to rest.
Some people find it useful to write a short diary every evening. You don't need to write much, just a few lines about your day.
And on day seven, think about what you've learned. Which changes do you want to keep making?
Remember to be patient with yourself. If you forget to follow a step, don't give up. Just start again the next day.
One last tip: stop to notice how you feel. Most people say they sleep better and feel less stressed after a week.
So, are you ready to try? Good luck, and see you on day one.

title: Two Weeks Before the Wedding

lines.text: Ben, the wedding's in two weeks. Can we check the list?
Sure. Let's start with the clothes. I'm having my suit altered on Thursday. The trousers are too long.
Good. My dress is ready, but I still need to get my shoes repaired. One of the heels is loose.
Didn't you buy those shoes for the wedding?
No, they were my mum's. That's why I'm having them fixed and not buying new ones.
That's lovely. What about the invitations? Did we have them printed in the end?
Yes, and we had them delivered by hand to your grandparents, because they don't trust the post.
Ha, that sounds like them. And the cake?
We're having it made by my cousin's bakery. It's chocolate and orange, your favourite.
Perfect. Now, the photos. Are we getting a professional photographer?
Yes, and I've asked him to take some photos at the beach before the ceremony.
Great. I also need to get my hair cut, but not too short this time.
Please have it done a few days before, not on the morning of the wedding!
Okay, okay. Oh, and what about the car? It's really dirty.
Get it washed on Friday. And please have the windows cleaned too.
Right. Suit, hair, car. I think I can remember that.

questions.q: I'm having my suit _____ on Thursday. The trousers are too long.
questions.explain_es: 'Have + objeto + participio' = otra persona lo hace por nosotros: 'I'm having my suit altered'.

questions.q: Use 'get something done': 'Someone needs to cut my hair.' → I also need to _____ (get / my hair / cut).
questions.explain_es: Estructura: get + objeto + participio. Ben: 'I also need to get my hair cut'.
